question: A patient on phenytoin for tonic-clonic seizures has a serum level of 25 µg/mL (therapeutic range: 10–20 µg/mL) after a small dose increase. She reports nystagmus and ataxia. What explains the disproportionate rise in plasma level?

answers.text: Phenytoin exhibits zero-order (saturation) kinetics at therapeutic concentrations — the metabolising enzyme is saturated, so small dose increases produce disproportionately large rises in plasma level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Phenytoin's hepatic hydroxylating enzyme (CYP2C9/CYP2C19) becomes saturated within the therapeutic range. Once saturated, the enzyme operates at maximum velocity (Vmax) — additional drug cannot be cleared faster, so even a 10% dose increase can double the plasma level. This is why therapeutic drug monitoring is mandatory.

answers.text: Phenytoin has first-order kinetics — the rise is proportional to the dose increase and is expected

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: If phenytoin had first-order kinetics, a 10% dose increase would produce a ~10% rise in plasma level. The clinical scenario shows a disproportionate rise (from therapeutic to toxic), which is characteristic of zero-order (saturation) kinetics — not first-order.

answers.text: Phenytoin undergoes auto-induction, which paradoxically reduces its own metabolism at higher doses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenytoin is actually a CYP enzyme inducer (it induces the metabolism of other drugs), but it does not undergo auto-induction. Its non-linear kinetics result from enzyme saturation, not induction effects.

answers.text: Phenytoin is 100% renally excreted — any dose above the renal threshold accumulates linearly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenytoin is almost entirely hepatically metabolised (>95%) by CYP2C9/CYP2C19, with negligible renal excretion of unchanged drug. The non-linearity is due to hepatic enzyme saturation, not renal handling.

overallFeedback.feedback: Zero-order kinetics means the rate of drug elimination is constant (at Vmax) regardless of drug concentration. Once saturated, the enzyme cannot eliminate additional drug any faster — plasma levels rise steeply with small dose increases. This is unique to phenytoin among common antiseizure drugs.

Phenytoin's zero-order kinetics at therapeutic doses makes it one of the most dangerous drugs to titrate. Always monitor serum levels (target 10–20 µg/mL) and make dose adjustments in small increments (25–50 mg).
